name: Capsaicin
lead: Capsaicin (8-methyl-N-vanillyl-6-nonenamide) is the main pungent compound in chili peppers. It and related capsaicinoids are produced by plants of the genus Capsicum, likely as a deterrent to mammals and fungi, and it causes a burning sensation on contact with tissues in mammals.[1]

It has two main relevant uses. As a prescription topical, a high-concentration (8%) patch (Qutenza) was approved by the US FDA and in the European Union in 2009 for pain from post-herpetic neuralgia and has since been studied in diabetic neuropathy.[1] In the fat-loss and supplement market, capsaicin and chili extracts are included in thermogenic products on the premise that they raise energy expenditure and fat oxidation or reduce appetite; Wikipedia reports that as of 2007 there was no evidence weight loss was directly correlated with ingesting it, and that a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that taking it before a meal might slightly reduce food intake.[1]
Capsaicin acts by binding the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing neurons, work that contributed to the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[1]

paras: Capsaicin is added to thermogenic fat-burner supplements and eaten in chilis in the belief that it increases heat production, fat oxidation and satiety. Researchers have measured these outcomes under controlled conditions, including acute energy expenditure and fat oxidation and substrate oxidation after modest weight loss.[5][6][7]

Topical capsaicin relieves some neuropathic pain by desensitising nociceptor fibres. A 2017 review described moderate to substantial relief of post-herpetic, HIV and diabetic neuropathic pain with the 8% preparation versus a 0.4% control, with limited quality of evidence, and the 12-week phase III trial in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy found a larger pain reduction with the 8% patch than placebo (about 27 percent versus 21 percent).[1][8] Reviews of neuropathic pain treatment and of painful diabetic neuropathy discuss capsaicin among the options.[9][10][11] Wikipedia notes insufficient evidence for itch (pruritus) and low-quality evidence that oral capsaicin may modestly lower LDL cholesterol.[1]

For weight: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials examined capsaicin intake in overweight and obese subjects, and a PLOS ONE study measured the acute effects of capsaicin on energy expenditure and fat oxidation; an earlier trial examined substrate oxidation and weight maintenance after modest weight loss.[5][6][7] Wikipedia reports that well-designed research has been hampered because the pungency of the doses used prevented participants from complying.[1]

For pain: the 8% patch trial enrolled 369 patients, with a shorter median time to response (19 versus 72 days) and modest improvements in sleep interference, and application-site reactions were the main adverse events apart from similar rates otherwise.[8] Other registered trials examine the patch in cancer-related neuropathic pain, post-surgical neuropathic pain, coccygodynia and amputation.[12][13][14] A 2024 randomized trial tested topical capsaicin for delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, and a 2015 trial tested its use in cough reduction.[15][16] Reviews of burning mouth syndrome treatment also include capsaicin.[17]

Capsaicin is a strong irritant of skin, eyes and airways. Ingesting large amounts can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and burning diarrhea, and eye exposure causes intense tearing and pain; Wikipedia also reports that ingestion of very high quantities can be fatal, particularly in people with heart problems, and that myocardial infarction has been reported after ingesting capsaicin capsules.[1] The reported LD50 in mice is 47.2 mg/kg.[1]
Plain water is ineffective at removing it from skin; alcohol dissolves it, and cold milk may relieve burning after ingestion.[1]

Capsaicin binds the TRPV1 ion channel on nociceptors, which is also activated by heat and protons, causing cation influx, depolarisation and sensations of burning. Prolonged activation leads to desensitisation or defunctionalisation of the fibres, which underlies its use as an analgesic.[1][3][4][19] TRPV1 was cloned in 1997 as a heat-activated ion channel in the pain pathway, and mice lacking it showed impaired pain sensation.[18][20]

Oral capsaicin is efficiently absorbed from the gut (85 percent in rats) but undergoes extensive first-pass liver metabolism. In human volunteers who ingested a Capsicum extract, the blood half-life was about 25 minutes with peak levels at 45 minutes. Topical capsaicin reaches the stratum corneum within a minute.[1]

Christian Friedrich Bucholz first extracted it in impure form in 1816, and Rudolf Buchheim (1873) and Endre Hogyes (1878) attributed the burning feeling to the substance.[1] It is used in food, in pepper sprays and in animal repellents. Capsaicin is banned in equestrian sports, and four horses were disqualified after testing positive at the 2008 Olympic show jumping events.[1]

timeline.event: Capsaicin first extracted in impure form by Christian Friedrich Bucholz.[1]
Rudolf Buchheim attributes the burning sensation to the extract.[1]
The capsaicin receptor (TRPV1) cloned as a heat-activated ion channel.[18]
Capsaicin 8% patch approved by FDA and EU for post-herpetic neuralgia pain.[1]
Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognises discovery of temperature and touch receptors, including work using capsaicin.[1]
